questions.q: What happens when an Azure Policy or RBAC role assignment is made at a management group level?
options: It only applies to resources created after the assignment, never to existing ones
It is inherited automatically by every subscription beneath that management group, with no per-subscription re-configuration needed
It must be manually copied to each subscription under that management group one at a time
It applies only to the Tenant Root Group itself and nowhere else
questions.explain: Management groups sit above subscriptions specifically so that policy and RBAC written once at that level reach every subscription underneath automatically.

questions.q: In the Azure Landing Zones reference architecture, what is the purpose of the Platform management group's Identity, Management, and Connectivity subscriptions?
options: They host shared infrastructure — identity, central logging/automation, and the hub network — that other subscriptions depend on but never run application workloads themselves
They exist as billing-only placeholders with no actual resources inside them
They run application workloads for the Corp landing zones
They are temporary subscriptions deleted once the tenant is fully onboarded
questions.explain: Platform subscriptions provide shared foundations (identity infrastructure, centralized Log Analytics/Automation, and the hub VNet with its gateways and firewall) that landing zone subscriptions rely on rather than rebuilding themselves.

questions.q: What distinguishes the Corp and Online sub-groups under Landing Zones in the reference architecture?
options: Corp subscriptions run only Windows workloads, while Online subscriptions run only Linux workloads
Online subscriptions are billed separately from the rest of the tenant
A policy distinction based on whether workloads need private, internally-facing connectivity (Corp) versus more direct internet exposure (Online)
Corp subscriptions are only used during a free trial period
questions.explain: The split is explicitly a policy distinction, not a technical limitation — it separates workloads by their connectivity exposure needs, and both still inherit policy and hub connectivity from the Platform subscriptions.

questions.q: What problem does subscription vending actually solve?
options: It lets a tenant avoid paying for Azure subscriptions by sharing one subscription across all teams
It replaces the need for any management group hierarchy at all
It encrypts subscription billing data so finance teams cannot see individual team costs
It exposes subscription creation as a parameterized, automated process, so a new subscription is provisioned already compliant and peered to the hub without being hand-built every time
questions.explain: Subscription vending keeps the thirtieth subscription exactly as compliant as the first by automating the same policy assignment and network peering steps every time, instead of relying on a human to repeat them correctly by hand.

questions.q: How does subscription vending typically relate to the Terraform skills already covered in Course 8?
options: It has no relationship — subscription vending is always done manually through the Azure portal
It applies the same Terraform module pattern from Course 8 at the subscription level, producing a compliant subscription from a small set of inputs instead of resource-level infrastructure
It replaces Terraform entirely with a proprietary Azure-only scripting language
It only works with AWS providers, not azurerm
questions.explain: The guide's Terraform module example shows subscription vending as the same declarative module pattern from Course 8, just operating one level up — on subscriptions rather than individual resources.
